thread.title: Alphabet Stock Slipped on a Mixed Earnings Report

title: Alphabet Stock Slipped on a Mixed Earnings Report
text:
Text size
Good but not good enough.
Alphabet (GOOGL) racked up third-quarter results that exceeded analyst expectations but not the sky-high bar it has set recently, including the previous quarter that propelled shares to an all-time high.
The parent of search-engine giant Google on Thursday reported $13.06 in adjusted earnings per share on $33.7 billion in revenue, eclipsing the $10.41 in adjusted EPS and $27.3 billion in revenue forecast by analysts polled by FactSet. A Refinitiv consensus estimate, however, was $34.04 billion. (In the same-quarter last year, Alphabet posted EPS of $9.57 on $22.3 billion in revenue.)
Its reward? An initial 7% drop in shares in after-hours trading, though shares have since rebounded a bit.
Since Alphabet shares hit an all-time high shortly after it reported second-quarter earnings in July , they’ve sunk below a 200-day moving average because of a market correction that savaged tech stocks.
And it will take nothing short of an innovative jolt to pick things up, say analysts. A top candidate is Google’s cloud-computing division, which Credit Suisse expected to produce $1.84 billion in third-quarter revenue.
“Core Google [search advertising revenue] remains solid, YouTube demand is strong, Google cloud is growing, and there are other emerging opportunities,” Macquarie analyst Benjamin Schachter writes in a note to clients. “However, we see limited known near-term catalysts and that may limit upside.”
Darkening the horizon are privacy and competitive obstacles. After spending much of the past year avoiding the klieg lights that shined brightly on Facebook (FB) and Twitter (TWTR) for data and security snafus, Google finds itself the center of regulatory attention following the disclosure that personal data for hundreds of thousands of Google+ users was potentially exposed because of a bug it kept quiet. The social network, which never gained much traction with consumers, was subsequently shut down .
Just as troubling, Google faces new threats for advertising dollars from Amazon.com (AMZN) and Apple (AAPL).
The company is also coping with an explosive New York Times story on Thursday that a few Google executives, including Android creator Andy Rubin, were shielded by the company from claims of sexual misconduct and paid large exit packages. Google CEO Sundar Pichai, in an email to employees later in the day, said Google had fired 48 people over two years for sexual harassment. He said 13 were “senior managers and above,” but none of them got big buyouts.
JPMorgan Chase analyst Doug Anmuth in a pre-earnings note this week had pointed to “increasing concerns of direct competition with Amazon’s fast-growing advertising business,” as well as broader ad industry data worries and increased regulatory scrutiny.
Still, there is plenty to like.
Google is the dominant leader in the $122.9 billion search market worldwide, with 59% share, says eMarketer.
Google is expected to capture a third of the $189.02 billion world-wide mobile ad market this year, followed by Facebook with 26.5% share, according to eMarketer.
Of 43 analysts who follow Alphabet, 39 have the equivalent of a buy rating on the stock and four a hold. Their average price target of $1,399.34 represents a 27% upside from Thursday’s close.
